Copper-Initiated Regiodivergent Chloropentafluorosulfanylation of
1,3-Enynes under Substrate Control
Lin Wang* and Wenhui Qin

ABSTRACT: A copper-catalyzed regiodivergent chloropentafluorosulfany-
lation strategy for 1,3-enynes using SF
5
Cl has been developed. The
regioselectivity is dictated by the structural and substitution patterns of
1,3-enynes, enabling facile access to three classes of SF
5
-containing products:
propargylic chlorides, 1,3-dienes, and allenes. The reaction systems involve
radical species, where the transfer of a chlorine atom from SF
5
Cl to a carbon
radical is considered the predominant pathway. Diverse types of SF
5
- building
blocks can be synthesized through simple functional group transformations.
T
he pentafluorosulfanyl group (SF
5
), a bioisostere of
trifluoromethyl group, possesses high electronegativity,
exceptional lipophilicity, superior chemical stability, and strong
metabolic robustness
1
owing to its distinctive square pyramidal
geometry and abundant fluorine atoms.
2
Besides enhancing
drug potency,
3
the incorporation of the SF
5
group also confers
benefits on the optoelectronic properties of materials
4
and the
activity of the parent catalysts
5
(Figure 1A). Therefore, the
growing demand for diversified multifunctional SF
5
-containing
structures necessitates the development of practical and
efficient synthetic methodologies. The state-of-the-art syn-
thetic strategy for access to aryl-SF
5
motifs involves the
stepwise oxidative fluorination of sulfur(II) precursors.
6
Alternatively, direct pentafluorosulfanylation reactions allowed
synthesis of aliphatic pentafluorosulfanylated compounds.
7
Pentafluorosulfanyl chloride (SF
5
Cl) is widely employed as a
reagent for direct pentafluorosulfanylation due to its optimal
balance between reactivity and stability.
8
Following the seminal
report of a user-friendly, gas-reagent free synthetic protocol by
Togni,
9
with subsequent contribution by Qing,
10
this reliable
source of SF
5
radical has become more manageable and
practical. The predominant method for introducing a SF
5
group involves the reactions of SF
5
Cl with alkenes or alkynes
via atom-transfer radical addition (ATRA) in the presence of
initiators such as BEt
3
.
11
In addition, it has been discovered
that SF
5
Cl exhibits reactivity toward α-diazo carbonyl
compounds, leading to the formation of α-SF
5
ketones and
esters
10,12
(Figure 1B). However, strategies for direct C−SF
5
bond formation remain limited to substrates containing only
one reactive site. In contrast, reports on reactions involving
more complex substrates featuring multiple reactive sites are
scarce,
13
where both regio- and chemoselectivity emerge as key
issues.
1,3-Enyne, a common molecule featuring conjugated double
and triple carbon−carbon bonds, exhibits multiple reactive
sites and can undergo diverse regioselective coupling reactions
such as 1,2-, 3,4-, and 1,4-functionalization.
14
Notably, the
radical addition strategy for difunctionalization of 1,3-enynes
via single-electron transfer offers significant advantages
including mild reaction conditions and excellent tolerance
toward functional groups.
15
Therefore, we designed a unified
protocol for accessing various valuable SF
5
-functionalized
products through the radical addition of SF
5
Cl to 1,3-enynes.
While conceptually simple, the implementation of this protocol
remains challenging. First, the steric hindrance and unique
electronic properties of SF
5
radical should be compatible with
the reactivity of 1,3-enynes; second, effective control over the
regioselectivity arising from multiple reactive sites in the
alkenyl and alkynyl positions remains unclear. Herein we
report on copper-initiated regiodivergent pentafluorosulfany-
lation of 1,3-enynes, which enables access to a wide range of
SF
5
-substituted propargylic derivatives, 1,3-dienes, and allenes,
where the regioselectivity is dictated by the intrinsic properties
of the enyne substrates (Figure 1C). Moreover, the resulting
SF
5
-containing building blocks can be further functionalized

We commenced our studies of chloropentafluoro-
sulfanylation using but-3-en-1-yn-1-ylbenzene (1a) as a
model substrate. Considering previous reports on metal-
catalyzed difunctionalization of 1,3-enynes,
14
we employed
copper catalysis to generate a SF
5
-radical and to initiate the
reaction. Following extensive optimization studies (see
Supporting Information), we eventually identified the optimal
conditions (Table 1, entry 1), under which 1a (1.0 equiv)
reacted with SF
5
Cl (0.075 M in hexane, 2.0 equiv), in the
presence of Cu(CH

the desired product 2a (90%) with excellent 1,2-selectivity as

19

During the optimization process, several noteworthy
observations were made. (1) The reactivity of the cationic
Cu(I) salt coordinated with a bipyridyl ligand outperformed
that of other Cu salts with a terpyridyl- or phenanthroline-type
ligand (Table 1, entries 2−6). (2) The addition of 0.75 mL of
diethyl ether proved to be indispensable, as deviations from its
loading caused detrimental effects on the reaction outcome
(Table 1, entries 7 and 8). Moreover, lower yields of 2a were
obtained when other solvents such as THF or dichloroethane
were used (Table 1, entries 9−11). This observation implies
that the specific Et
2
O to hexane ratio facilitates the
compatibility of SF
5
radical with the reactivity of 1,3-enyne.
(3) By employing the well-established Et

ditions,

only a poor yield was achieved for the 1,2-addition
product (Table 1, entry 12).
With the optimized conditions in hand, we proceeded to
investigate the scope of this chloropentafluorosulfanylation
system using a series of 4-substituted 1,3-enynes (Scheme 1).
These substrates, possessing a terminal olefin moiety, exhibited
exclusive 1,2-selectivity and delivered the corresponding SF
5
-
substituted propargylic chlorides in high yields. Notably, both
the substitution pattern and the electronic nature of the aryl
groups exerted negligible influence on either the yields or
regioselectivity (2a−2p). This protocol also demonstrated
excellent compatibility with typical functional groups such as
ester (2q), ketone (2r), aldehyde (2s), and cyano (2t) groups.
Among the examples examined, only a substrate bearing a para
alkynyl group reacted with low conversion (2u), albeit with
consistently excellent regioselectivity. Heteroaryl substituents
such as a thienyl or benzofuryl were also well tolerated (2v and
2w). Moreover, the alkynyl terminus was also smoothly
extended to different alkyl groups (2x and 2y).
To further investigate the scope of the enyne substrates, we
employed 4-unsubstituted enynes, which exhibited distinct
regioselectivity (Scheme 2). Under identical reaction con-
ditions as in Scheme 1, (E)-but-1-en-3-yn-1-ylbenzene (3a)
selectively coupled with 4,3-regioselectivity to afford the 4a in
73% yield. Additionally, minor side-products resulting from
dichlorination at positions 3 and 4 were also observed. The
observed outcomes highlight the significant steric effect around
the reactive sites influencing regioselectivity. Subsequent
investigation using various 4-unsubstituted 1,3-enynes revealed

para nitro group into the aryl ring resulted in a lower yield for
this reaction (4h, 32%), indicating sensitivity of these
substrates toward electronic perturbation. The steric effect
also governs the mutual trans orientation between the SF

Intriguingly, both 1,1- and 1,2-disubsituted enynes (3i−3k),
including a cyclene-containing enyne (3l), underwent smooth
transformation into the desired 4,3-addition products (4i−4l).
Having observed the pronounced substrate-dependent
selectivity, we proceeded to investigate the chloropentafluoro-
sulfanylation reaction of a series of 2,4- and 1,4-disubstituted
1,3-enynes with different substituents (Scheme 3). While a
methyl group at the 2-position had minimal impact on the
formation of 1,2-difunctionalization product 8, bulkier groups
such as phenyl caused a remarkable switch toward 1,4-
selectivity (Scheme 3, reaction 2). Consequently, enyne 6
containing a phenyl and a linear alkyl at the 2- and 4-position
respectively reacted through the 1,4-addition pathway,
resulting in new-style SF
5
-substituted allene 9 as the exclusive
F-containing product. In this case, formation of a propargyl
radical with subsequent radical isomerization
16
may occur, and
the relatively bulky steric substituent disfavors the radical
chlorine atom transfer to the 2-position carbon. Regarding 1,4-
disubstituted enyne substrate 7, both propargyl chloride (10)
and diene product (11) were obtained in a 1.3:1 ratio, which
suggests that the substituents at the 1-position decreased the
regioselectivity of 1,2- versus 3,4-addition.
Experimental studies have been conducted to gain
mechanistic insight into this chloropentafluorosulfanylation
system (Scheme 4). First, the introduction of a 2,2,6,6-
tetramethyl-1-piperidinoxyl (TEMPO) effectively inhibited the
reaction. Meanwhile, radical trapping studies using 1,1-
diphenylethene further supported the formation of SF
5
and
Cl radical (Scheme 4A). More compelling evidence for
involvement of organic radicals was obtained from the radical
clock experiment (Scheme 4B), where a ring-opened
difunctionalization product 14 was detected in 27% yield,
while only traces of the 1,2-addition product 13 were observed.
This suggests that the steric hindrance at the 2-position in
enynes plays a crucial role in the chlorine-atom transfer. In
order to investigate the potential pathway of chlorine atom
transfer, we investigated the effect of the 4-silyl group in 4-
substituted 1,3-enynes on the regioselectivity. Unlike the aryl-
or alkyl-substituted substrates, the chloropentafluoro-
sulfanylation of compounds 15 proceeded in high total yields
(78−83%) to give a mixture of 1,2- and 1,4-addition products.
Notably, when the steric hindrance around the silicon atom is
minimal (15a and 15b), an ∼1:1 ratio of propargyl chlorides
(16a and 16b) and allenes (16a′ and 16b′) was observed.
Conversely, with increased steric hindrance around the silicon
atom (15c), the major product corresponds to the 1,2-addition
(16c) with a ratio of 8:1. Since these silyl groups exhibit similar
electron effects, we rationalized that this trend of regiose-
lectivity likely arises from interactions between the fluorine
atom in SF
5
Cl and the silicon atom in the substrates during the
intermolecular chlorine atom transfer from SF
5
Cl to the carbon
radical.
A plausible reaction pathway is proposed based on the above
mechanistic experiment results and literature (Scheme 4D).
The single electron transfer (SET) reaction between SF
5
Cl and
a Cu(I) complex gives a SF
5
radical and a Cu(II)−Cl species.

allenyl radical (A′). Generally, Cl atom transfer occurred more
rapidly than isomerization (B), resulting in the formation of
1,2-addition products. However, when a bulky substituent is
present at the 2-position of enyne or when substituents at the
4-position interact with SF
5

preferentially occurs at the 4-position (B′), affording SF

Our direct pentafluorosulfanylation strategy demonstrated
good synthetic values. Two reactions were scalable to a 1
mmol scale, giving the desired products in 60% and 46% yields
for 2j and 4a, respectively (Scheme 5A). Furthermore,
hydrodechlorination of 2, in the presence of 2,2′-azobis(2-
methylpropionitrile (AIBN) and tributyltin hydride,
17
resulted
in high-yielding synthesis of the corresponding alkyne 17
(Scheme 5B). Increasing the loading of tributyltin hydride led
to further hydrostannation of the alkyne
18
to give two
regioisomeric olefins with a ratio of 5.3:1 (Scheme 5C).
Alternatively, treatment of 1,3-diene 4a with a strong base
19
provided the 4-SF
5
-substituted 1,3-enyne via elimination of a
HCl (Scheme 5D).
In conclusion, we have developed a copper-initiated
regiodivergent chloropentafluorosulfanylation of 1,3-enynes
using SF
5
Cl as the reagent. The regioselectivity of this system
is dictated by the structural characteristics of the enyne
substrates. Specifically, substrates containing a terminal olefin
were selectively converted to the corresponding SF
5
-
substituted propargylic chlorides. For the 4-unsubstituted
1,3-enynes, only SF
5
-substituted 1,3-dienes were obtained.
When the substituents at the 2-position were bulkier than
those at the 4-position, allenes bearing the SF
5
group became
the major products. Regarding the reaction mechanism, the
potential pathway of chlorine atom transfer from SF
5
Cl to the
carbon radical seems predominant. The novel
chloropentafluorosulfanylation products can be transformed
into various SF
5
-containing building blocks through different
methods, with potential applications in synthetic chemistry.
